newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU stresses need for single market action.
newsitem.headline: EU stresses need for single market action.

text.p: The European Commission won broad political backing from European Union internal trade ministers on Thursday for its efforts to put together an ambitious action plan for completing the single market by 1999.

Ministers debated a report by the EU executive which showed that the single market had boosted growth and jobs since it was launched in 1993 but that many holes remained to be plugged to make it work properly.
"There is agreement on the need for a renewed commitment to the internal market," said Michiel Patijn, Dutch state secretary for foreign affairs, who chaired the meeting.

The European Commission, eager to boost jobs and competitiveness, is preparing an action plan for the completion of the single market which will be presented to a summit of EU leaders in Amsterdam on June 16-17.
Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti said it would be a "major political initiative" in order to achieve concrete results in a short period of time.

He said there may be new legislative proposals to boost the single market but that it was equally important to agree steps to fully implement and enforce existing legislation at the national level, to simplify rules and to boost information.

During the debate, most ministers voiced support for the Commission's report and its preparations for the action programme, which is designed to ensure that the single market is fully in place at the same time as monetary union.
"The action plan should emphasise the need for an open single market which facilitates trade and competitiveness on a global scale," said David Bostock, Britain's deputy EU ambassador.
However, ministers also highlighted different priorities -- reflecting different attitudes among member states.
For example, while the Nordic and British representatives stressed the need to clamp down on state aid, France and Belgium underlined the necessity to take into account social and employment aspects.

"Doing things too narrowly from the internal market point of view...can in certain cases lead to a certain amount of inconsistency in policy and situations which are really not very acceptable from the human point of view," said French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier.
Referring to recent truckers' strikes in France and Spain as well as plans by carmaker Renault to cut staff, Barnier added:
"We as ministers responsible for the Union are obviously affected by the apparent impotence of Europe to get to grips with all the different dimensions of the single market."
The Belgium representative took a similar line and condemned as "scandalous and immoral" the way Renault had announced plans to close its Vilvoorde plant outside Brussels.
"In the future we have to prevent this from happening again," Belgian deputy EU ambassador Luc Carbonez said.
Danish Trade and Industry Minister Jan Trojberg underlined that state aid must be reduced. "State aid must be limited to what is strictly needed," he told the meeting.
There was also a need to ensure a single market in new and expanding industries, such as in the biotechnology and the information technology sectors, ministers said.
